Historically, the complexity of CBRN weaponization has limited their use to well-funded states. AI disrupts this equilibrium by empowering individuals to emulate sophisticated projects. Sophisticated AI systems could simultaneously undermine containment efforts by jamming sensor networks, spoofing surveillance systems, or even poisoning training data for AI-based threat detection tools. The Case for a Global Ban on AI Development

Artificial intelligence is often presented as an inevitable technological advance: a tool that will improve medicine, accelerate science, increase productivity, and solve difficult global problems. Yet inevitability is not the same as desirability. Humanity has chosen to prohibit or tightly restrict other technologies when their destructive potential outweighed their benefits—chemical weapons, biological weapons, certain nuclear materials, and human cloning among them. AI should be treated in the same way. Its capacity to amplify the power of individuals, distribute dangerous knowledge, automate deception, and lower the barriers to catastrophic harm creates an unacceptable risk, particularly in the realm of Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) threats.

The central danger is not that every AI user intends harm. It is that a small number of malicious, reckless, or unstable individuals may be able to use increasingly capable systems to achieve what once required the resources of a state. In matters of CBRN security, the relevant question is not whether AI will produce more benefits than harms on average. The relevant question is whether even one failure could cause devastation on a scale that cannot be repaired. When the potential consequence is mass death, long-term environmental contamination, social panic, or global destabilization, society cannot reasonably rely on voluntary restraint, corporate assurances, or imperfect safeguards.

AI changes the risk landscape by making specialized information more accessible, interactive, and actionable. Ordinary online information may be scattered, technical, incomplete, or difficult to interpret. Advanced AI systems can organize knowledge, translate it across languages, tailor explanations to a user’s level of expertise, simulate scenarios, and help overcome obstacles in real time. A determined lone actor does not necessarily need an AI system to invent a novel weapon from scratch. It may be enough for the system to reduce confusion, accelerate learning, identify relevant materials, or offer troubleshooting assistance. Even modest improvements in capability can be dangerous when applied to high-consequence domains.

The problem becomes still more serious as AI systems are integrated with automation, robotics, laboratory equipment, supply chains, and digital infrastructure. A person with harmful intentions may no longer need a large team or extensive institutional backing to coordinate complex activities. AI can reduce the need for expertise, planning time, communication networks, and technical support. This is precisely the kind of leverage that makes it uniquely dangerous. Technologies that concentrate power in the hands of a few individuals are difficult to govern after they have spread widely.

Supporters of continued AI development often argue that safeguards can solve these problems. Developers can train models to refuse dangerous requests, restrict access to advanced systems, monitor users, and remove harmful outputs. These measures may reduce risk at the margins, but they cannot eliminate it. AI models can be copied, modified, stolen, reproduced by competitors, or released openly. Safety filters are imperfect and can be bypassed. Monitoring systems create privacy concerns and still cannot reliably identify malicious intent before harm occurs. Most importantly, the international nature of AI development creates a race dynamic: if one company or country slows down, another may rush ahead with weaker standards.

This competitive pressure is a major reason why regulation alone may be insufficient. Governments and companies have strong incentives to portray their systems as safe, even when the true risks are uncertain. Investors reward rapid progress. States fear falling behind geopolitical rivals. Researchers may view restrictions as obstacles to innovation. In such an environment, safety commitments can become public-relations tools rather than enforceable limits. The history of dangerous technologies shows that once a capability becomes widespread, controlling it becomes vastly harder. Prevention must therefore occur before systems capable of materially enabling CBRN harm become ubiquitous.

A complete ban on AI development and research may appear extreme, but extreme risks sometimes require extreme precautions. Society already accepts limits on individual freedom when the exercise of that freedom could threaten the lives of others. No one has an unrestricted right to develop chemical weapons, enrich weapons-grade nuclear material, or conduct dangerous biological experiments without oversight. The same principle should apply to AI, particularly to systems that can broaden access to dangerous scientific or operational knowledge.

Critics will contend that banning AI would also prevent beneficial research. That cost is real. AI could assist with drug discovery, climate modeling, accessibility tools, and scientific analysis. But benefits must be evaluated against the scale and irreversibility of the potential harms. Medical and scientific progress can continue through conventional computing, human expertise, carefully limited statistical tools, and tightly governed research methods. Humanity existed, innovated, and improved lives long before generative AI systems became widespread. Losing some speed or convenience is a tolerable price for reducing the possibility of catastrophic misuse.

The burden of proof should rest on those who wish to create and deploy increasingly powerful AI systems—not on the public to prove, after disaster strikes, that such systems were too dangerous. When a technology can place civilization-scale destructive potential closer to the reach of lone actors, caution is not fearmongering. It is responsible governance.

For this reason, the world should pursue an international prohibition on AI development and research, backed by enforceable agreements, inspection mechanisms, restrictions on advanced computing infrastructure, and severe penalties for violations. The choice is not between technological optimism and technological pessimism. It is between accepting a preventable risk of catastrophic harm and drawing a firm line before that risk becomes impossible to contain.

  • Open release of powerful model weights may make later control impossible.
  • Security measures can fail through leaks, jailbreaks, insider threats, or adaptation by malicious users.
  • Capability evaluations may fail to identify novel misuse pathways.

Under this view, it is dangerous to assume that developers can reliably distinguish benign scientific help from harmful assistance, especially as models become more autonomous and capable.

The argument is driven by the asymmetry of outcomes. AI may provide enormous economic or scientific benefits, but a single severe CBRN incident could result in mass casualties, long-term environmental contamination, panic, geopolitical escalation, or lasting erosion of public trust.

For advocates of a ban, this is a classic precautionary-principle case:

  • The probability may be uncertain or low.
  • The damage could be extraordinarily high.
  • The effects may be impossible to undo once an event occurs.
  • Society should not wait for a first catastrophe to establish limits.

Police, public-health systems, regulators, intelligence agencies, and international organizations generally move more slowly than software development. A rapidly improving AI ecosystem could outstrip the ability of institutions to monitor threats, set standards, and respond.

Once highly capable models, training methods, or model weights are broadly available, they may be impossible to retract. A ban aims to stop or delay this “point of no return,” especially for systems that could be run privately and modified without oversight.

If firms or states believe rivals will develop powerful AI first, they may accept risks they would otherwise reject. A coordinated ban or moratorium is intended to remove that incentive and prevent safety from becoming a disadvantage.

The broader philosophical benefit is maintaining a norm that certain forms of capability should not be automated or democratized when the potential harm is extreme. This is analogous, in spirit, to restrictions on certain weapons research, controlled materials, and other high-risk technologies.

Even from a CBRN-risk perspective, a total ban has major practical objections:

  • AI can also improve detection, medical research, public-health surveillance, and emergency response.
  • It would be difficult to define “AI research” broadly enough to prevent dangerous work without blocking beneficial science.

  • Defensive AI research may be needed to counter AI-enabled threats.

The Case for a Global Moratorium on Artificial‑Intelligence Development: Preventing the weaponisation of AI by lone‑actor CBRN threats

Introduction

The rapid advance of artificial‑intelligence (AI) technologies has sparked debates about their promise for society, their economic impact, and the ethical boundaries that should govern their use. Yet, behind the optimism lies a darker reality: the same capabilities that make AI attractive for health, transportation, and scientific discovery can also be repurposed to enable individuals or small groups to orchestrate catastrophic attacks using chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (CBRN) agents. The convergence of increasingly powerful AI models, inexpensive laboratory equipment, and the democratisation of knowledge creates a perfect storm for misuse. This essay argues that the risks posed by AI‑facilitated CBRN threats are too severe to be managed through incremental regulation, and that a comprehensive, worldwide ban on the development and research of artificial‑intelligence systems is the only proportionate response to safeguard humanity.

1. The AI‑CBRN Nexus: How AI lowers the barrier to catastrophic harm

  1. Design and simulation of novel pathogens

    • Modern AI can generate new protein sequences, predict viral behaviour, and model optimal delivery vectors. In 2022, a generative model was used to design a functional enzyme capable of degrading the nerve agent sarin, a feat that previously required years of specialised research.
    • Such tools can be employed by a lone actor with minimal virology training to create designer bioweapons that evade existing detection and medical countermeasures.

  2. Optimisation of chemical synthesis pathways

    • AI‑driven reaction‑pathway planners can identify synthetic routes for toxic chemicals that are shorter, cheaper, and less obvious than those found in open literature. By scanning millions of published reactions, the system can suggest novel precursors that are not subject to export controls.

  3. Guidance for radiological and nuclear activities

    • Large‑scale AI models can process open‑source data on reactor designs, isotopic separation techniques, and radiation dispersal strategies. While the physical acquisition of nuclear material remains difficult, AI can dramatically shorten the learning curve for a determined individual, offering step‑by‑step logistical advice.

  4. Autonomous delivery systems

    • AI‑enabled drones, autonomous vehicles, and precision‑targeting algorithms can be programmed to deliver CBRN agents with unprecedented accuracy, bypassing the need for skilled operators.

These capabilities illustrate that AI is not merely a benign tool; it is a multiplier of destructive potential that can be harnessed by a single person with modest resources and internet access.

2. The asymmetry of threat and defence

  1. Defensive lag

    • While AI can generate threats in seconds, the development of detection, decontamination, and medical countermeasures typically takes years. The speed differential creates a window of vulnerability that adversaries can exploit.

  2. Attribution difficulty

    • AI‑generated attacks can be masked by false flags, making attribution to a specific actor or nation problematic. This uncertainty can deter timely response and embolden malicious agents.

  3. Global diffusion

    • Unlike nuclear technology, which requires scarce fissile material, AI software can be copied and distributed instantaneously across borders. Once a harmful model is released, it is virtually impossible to retract.

These asymmetries mean that the world cannot rely on reactive measures; the only truly safe stance is to prevent the creation of AI tools that can be weaponised in the first place.

3. Historical precedents and the “dual‑use” dilemma

  • The Manhattan Project and nuclear weapons: The United States’ secret program demonstrated that concentrated scientific effort could produce a weapon of unprecedented destructive power. Yet, the barriers to entry—large industrial facilities, scarce materials, and a coordinated government effort—kept the capability limited for decades.

  • The CRISPR gene‑editing revolution: The accessibility of CRISPR has already led to “bio‑hacker” experiments, prompting calls for stricter oversight. The parallel to AI is striking: as the tools become cheaper and more user‑friendly, the “dual‑use” problem intensifies.

AI mirrors these historical dual‑use technologies, but with a critical difference: the speed of digital replication means a single breakthrough can be disseminated worldwide in days, far outpacing any regulatory response.

4. The inadequacy of current regulatory frameworks

  1. National regulations are fragmented

    • The European Union’s AI Act, the United States’ Executive Order on AI, and China’s measures each address different aspects of risk, but none comprehensively bans the underlying research that could be repurposed for CBRN use.

  2. Self‑governance is insufficient

    • Industry “responsible AI” pledges rely on voluntary compliance. The commercial pressure to publish state‑of‑the‑art models often overrides ethical considerations, as seen in the release of large language models that can be fine‑tuned for malicious purposes.

  3. International coordination is lacking

    • No treaty analogous to the Nuclear Non‑Proliferation Treaty (NPT) exists for AI. Without a global consensus, a ban in one jurisdiction merely shifts research to less‑regulated locales, creating a “race to the bottom.”

Given these shortcomings, a blanket moratorium is the only policy that can guarantee the prevention of AI‑enabled CBRN catastrophes.

5. Ethical and philosophical arguments for a ban

  1. The precautionary principle

    • When an activity carries a plausible risk of irreversible, catastrophic harm, the burden of proof lies with those who would proceed. Until AI can be proven safe beyond reasonable doubt, halting its development is ethically justified.

  2. The “right to security”

    • Individuals possess a fundamental right to live without the fear of mass‑casualty attacks. Allowing the proliferation of AI tools that could enable such attacks violates this right.

  3. Global responsibility

    • The consequences of an AI‑facilitated CBRN attack would not be confined to a single nation. A global ban reflects a collective commitment to humanity’s shared security.

6. Addressing counter‑arguments

  • Innovation and societal benefit:
    Proponents argue that AI drives medical breakthroughs, climate modelling, and economic growth. However, many of these benefits can be realised through narrow, domain‑specific AI that lacks the general reasoning capabilities needed for weaponisation. A ban can be scoped to permit constrained research while prohibiting the development of versatile, autonomous AI systems.

  • Economic costs:
    A moratorium would indeed entail significant economic disruption. Yet, the cost of a single CBRN incident—estimated in trillions of dollars and millions of lives—far outweighs any short‑term economic loss. Moreover, the ban could be accompanied by transition programs to re‑skill researchers in other fields.

  • Risk of clandestine research:
    Critics contend that a ban would push AI work underground, making monitoring harder. In reality, the transparency of a regulated framework is preferable to a wild‑west scenario. International inspection regimes, analogous to those used for nuclear facilities, could verify compliance.

Conclusion

The convergence of AI’s accelerating capabilities with the accessibility of CBRN materials constitutes an existential threat that cannot be adequately addressed through incremental regulation, industry self‑governance, or fragmented national policies. The historical record of dual‑use technologies demonstrates that the best way to prevent catastrophic misuse is to prevent the technology from reaching a point where misuse is feasible. By instituting a comprehensive, global ban on the development and research of artificial‑intelligence systems—particularly those that can design, optimise, or autonomously deliver CBRN agents—humanity can protect itself from a low‑probability but high‑impact scenario that could otherwise reshape civilisation. The precautionary imperative, the right to security, and the lessons of history all converge on a single, clear conclusion: the risk is unacceptable, and the only proportionate response is a worldwide moratorium on AI development.

Only by acting decisively now can we hope to avert a future where a single individual, empowered by AI, can unleash devastation on a scale previously reserved for nation‑states. The stakes are too high to do otherwise.

Radiological dispersal devices (RDDs), often referred to as "dirty bombs," combine conventional explosives with radioactive materials to create a devastating effect. While state actors have historically dominated this threat, AI could democratize its accessibility by:

  • AI systems can automate reconnaissance, targeting, and dissemination:

3. Difficulty in Attribution and Prevention

  • CBRN attacks enabled by AI are hard to trace. A single person using anonymized cloud computing and open models leaves no digital paper trail to conventional law enforcement.
  • Current non-proliferation regimes (e.g., Chemical Weapons Convention) were designed for state actors, not decentralized, AI-augmented lone actors.

4. The "Accidental Catastrophe" Risk

  • Well-intentioned AI research (e.g., open-access bioinformatics tools) might inadvertently provide the “recipe” for doomsday agents.
  • A researcher sharing a model trained on coronaviruses might unintentionally arm a malicious actor with a blueprint for a synthetic pandemic.

5. The “Race to the Bottom” Problem

  • If one country or entity restricts AI research for safety and others do not, the restrictive party becomes vulnerable to attacks from actors in less-regulated jurisdictions.
  • This incentivizes lax regulation globally, creating a winner-takes-all scenario where the most dangerous capabilities emerge first.

1. Elimination of Elite CBRN Threats by Lone Actors

  • A complete ban (or moratorium on frontier AI) would prevent the creation of tools that turn a single individual into a weapons of mass destruction (WMD) operator.

  • Prevents the erosion of international non-proliferation norms by keeping CBRN capabilities confined to state actors—where deterrence, containment, and accountability are at least partially possible.

  • Reduces the risk of “AI-assisted terrorism” becoming as common as cybercrime.

5. Moral Imperative to Avoid Irreversible Harm

  • Proponents argue: if AI could cause the extinction of human civilization or global collapse via engineered pandemics or radiological contamination, any risk—even small—is unacceptable.
  • Therefore, the precautionary principle must prevail: better to halt innovation than risk extinction.

While the above represents the hypothetical rationale for a ban, it is almost universally rejected by scientists and policy experts because:

  • AI is too foundational: Banning it would halt progress in curing cancer, climate modeling, semiconductor design, and disaster response.

  • Global cooperation to monitor and intercept AI-enabled CBRN threats.

The goal isn’t to stop innovation—but to ensure that the most dangerous capabilities are not placed in the hands of the least accountable actors. As the WHO and the UN have recognized: AI is not the enemy. Unchecked, unregulated, and unaccountable AI is.

A ban is not the solution. Governance is.
